opus-5.5.text:
I think the value of a large team really shows up when something goes wrong, and in model training things go wrong all the time. A loss spike, a sudden drop on some benchmark, a model that looks fine on paper but behaves strangely when you actually talk to it. These problems rarely have a single obvious cause. It could be the data, the infrastructure, a numerical issue, an evaluation bug, or some subtle interaction between all of them.

When you have a larger team, you can attack the problem from many directions at once. One person is checking the data pipeline, another is going through the training logs, someone else is rerunning a smaller-scale experiment to see if it reproduces. Investigation that would take one person weeks can collapse into a few days. That speed matters a lot, because compute is expensive, and every day you're stuck is a day you're either burning resources or sitting idle.

There's also a diversity-of-intuition benefit. Different people have been burned by different bugs. Someone who has spent years on infrastructure will smell a hardware or communication issue immediately, while someone from the data side will notice a distribution shift that others overlook. Putting those perspectives in the same room often gets you to the root cause faster than any single brilliant person could.

That said, I don't think "large" by itself is the point. A large team only helps if information flows well. If people are siloed, or afraid to say "I think this might be my bug," the size actually works against you, because problems get hidden or duplicated. What you really want is a team where everyone feels ownership of the whole model, not just their own piece, and where it's normal to share half-formed hypotheses early. In that kind of culture, scale becomes a real advantage. Without it, you just have more people waiting for someone else to figure it out.

So to me, the large team is valuable as a kind of parallel debugging engine, but the engine only runs well if the culture is open, the tooling makes experiments easy to reproduce, and people trust each other enough to move fast together.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a large team can work against problem solving when people are siloed, and that more people may end up waiting for someone else to figure things out.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people often underestimate this. When I was at DeepSeek, and even more so now at Xiaomi, a lot of what we do during a training run is actually debugging rather than inventing. A large model is such a complex system that when the loss curve behaves strangely, or when a downstream capability doesn't emerge as expected, the cause could sit anywhere: in the data pipeline, in the tokenizer, in a numerical issue inside the kernel, in the optimizer, in the parallelism strategy, or in the evaluation itself. No single person can hold all of these layers in their head with enough depth to localize the problem quickly.

So the value of a large team, to me, is not that you have more hands. It's that you have people who each live inside one layer and have very sharp intuition there. When something goes wrong, you put them in a room and within a day you can rule out five hypotheses that would have taken one brilliant researcher two weeks to test one by one. In pretraining, time is compute, and compute is extremely expensive, so that speed of diagnosis is directly worth money.

But I also want to be honest about the other side. A large team only has this value if the information flows. If people are organized so that the data team doesn't know what the infrastructure team changed last week, the size actually becomes a liability, because now the problem space has more hidden variables. So when we build a team, I care a lot about whether everyone can see the same dashboards, read the same experiment logs, and feel free to say "I think the issue is on my side." The culture of being willing to own a mistake quickly matters more than the headcount.

And finally, there's a creative benefit. Many of the ideas that end up mattering in our models didn't come from a planned research direction. They came from someone noticing an anomaly while fixing something else and asking why. With more people looking at the system from different angles, you get more of these accidental observations. A small team can be very efficient, but it tends to see the problem through only a few lenses. A large team, if it's well connected, sees the whole elephant.

r001.rationale: The response says a large team can become a liability when information does not flow, because it adds hidden variables to diagnosing training problems.

astra-6.text:
I think the value of a large team lies in being able to look at the same problem from different perspectives. When something goes wrong during training, you often don’t know immediately whether it comes from the data, the model architecture, the optimization process, or the underlying infrastructure. People with different expertise can investigate those possibilities in parallel and challenge one another’s assumptions.

But having more people doesn’t automatically mean you solve problems faster. You need clear hypotheses, well-designed experiments, and a way to share what you’ve learned—including what didn’t work. Otherwise, people may repeat the same experiments or make changes whose effects are hard to separate. For me, the real advantage is turning individual observations into a shared understanding, so the whole team can narrow down the cause and move forward together.

r001.rationale: The response says more people do not automatically solve problems faster and may repeat experiments or make changes whose effects are hard to separate, communicating a potential disadvantage of a large team.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value of a large team is that you can bring different perspectives to the same problem. During model training, you might see a metric change, but that alone doesn’t tell you whether the cause is the data, the training setup, or something in the infrastructure. People with different expertise can investigate those possibilities in parallel and challenge each other’s assumptions.

But having more people doesn’t automatically make you faster. You need a shared understanding of the problem, clear ownership, and a way to share experimental results. Otherwise, people may repeat the same work or draw conclusions from different conditions. The real advantage is turning individual discoveries into knowledge the whole team can use.

r001.rationale: The response says more people do not automatically make problem-solving faster and explains that poor coordination can lead to duplicated work or conflicting conclusions, communicating a potential disadvantage of a large team.
